settings.title: Stream codec
settings.help: H.264 costs a fraction of the bandwidth of MJPEG on a screen that barely changes, and about a third of the frame rate. Browsers decode it through WebCodecs, which they offer on HTTPS pages only, so it is unusable over plain HTTP until TLS is in place.

settings.title: JPEG quality
settings.help: Higher is sharper and larger. Only affects the MJPEG codec.

settings.title: H.264 bitrate
settings.help: Target bitrate for the hardware encoder.

settings.title: Allow WebRTC
settings.help: Let the console take H.264 over WebRTC: UDP, so a lost packet costs one frame instead of holding up the ones behind it. Only a signed-in console can start it, and the video is encrypted (DTLS-SRTP). Off sends all video over the WebSocket.

settings.title: Frame rate limit
settings.help: Upper bound on encoded frames per second. Lower it to save bandwidth on a slow link.

settings.title: Skip unchanged frames
settings.help: Stop sending while the target's screen is static. Drops the bitrate to nearly zero on an idle desktop. MJPEG only: H.264 already codes an unchanged screen as a frame of a few hundred bytes.

settings.title: Rebuild a stuck H.264 encoder
settings.help: The encoder's rate controller can settle at its coarsest setting and stay there: the picture goes to visible blocks on a screen that is not moving, and nothing short of building a new encoder brings it back. With this on, keyframes that collapse to a fraction of their usual size are taken as that fault and the encoder is rebuilt - a lost frame, once every two minutes at most. Turn it off if a screen of yours is being rebuilt for no reason; the log says when it happens.

settings.title: EDID profile
settings.help: What this device claims to be, as a monitor - the target picks its output mode from what is offered here. "Full" advertises the common modes from 640x480 up to 1920x1080@30. "720p" and "1024x768" stop lower, which is often what you want: a smaller picture encodes faster and costs less bandwidth. "1080p30" offers that one mode alone, for a source that refuses a list. "480p" offers 720x480 and nothing bigger, for old consoles and TV boxes. "1080p50", the default, is "Full" with 1920x1080@50 first: the target sends a frame every 20 ms instead of 33, so the pointer shows up sooner, for a frame or two a second less. Only boards with a rev 3.x chip and a TC358743 take 50 Hz; others get "Full". Text modes stay on offer either way, so a BIOS still comes through as text.

settings.title: New recording file every
settings.help: A long recording is written as several files, each playable on its own, so one is quick to download and a damaged card loses one piece rather than the whole. 0 starts a new file only at 3.9 GB, the largest file the device writes.

settings.title: Stop a recording after
settings.help: So a recording left running does not fill the card. 0 records until it is stopped or the card is full. A runbook's "record <seconds>" and the API's ?seconds= set their own length instead.

settings.title: Keep the last minutes in memory
settings.help: Keeps the screen's recent past in memory, and saves it to the microSD card as a clip when something happens - the screen stays one colour, a watched phrase appears, the power goes off - or when you press Save clip. How far back depends on the picture: minutes of a still screen, seconds of a playing video. Needs H.264, and keeps the encoder running while it is on. On boards with an older (pre-3.0) chip there is less memory left, so it reaches back seconds, not minutes; keep the past on the microSD card there instead.

settings.title: Where the past is kept
settings.help: "Memory" holds what PSRAM can spare and does not touch the card until something happens. "microSD" writes the screen to the card all the time, in 15-second pieces in VIDEO/.dashcam, and deletes the old ones: it reaches back as far as the setting below on any board, but the card cannot be handed to the target meanwhile.

settings.title: Before the event
settings.help: At most this much of the past goes into a clip - if memory holds that much, or all of it when the past is kept on the card.

settings.title: After the event
settings.help: How long a clip goes on after what set it off. Another event meanwhile makes it longer, up to ten minutes in all.

settings.title: Save when the screen stays one colour
settings.help: Half a minute of one flat colour, such as a stop screen. A black screen does not count: that is usually the display going to sleep.

settings.title: Save when a watched phrase appears
settings.help: The phrases are the ones set for screen alerts.

settings.title: Save when the target's power goes off
settings.help: Needs the ATX power LED wired, so the device can see it.

settings.title: Save the screen's text with a recording
settings.help: Reads the screen as characters every few seconds while recording and writes what it says into a .txt beside the video, so the recordings panel can search it and jump to the moment. Only screens drawn as text can be read - a BIOS, an installer, a console - and reading one costs about a tenth of a second.

settings.title: Timelapse: a frame every
settings.help: What a timelapse started from Home Assistant, or offered first in the recordings panel, keeps: one frame this often, played back at 25 fps.

settings.title: Keystrokes in recordings
settings.help: Writes what was pressed as subtitles next to each recording (a .srt file of the same name; VLC and mpv show it). "Keys": shortcuts, named keys and clicks, with typed characters shown as dots. "Everything": the typed text too - which includes any password typed on the target, stored on the card in plain text.

settings.title: Mouse clicks in recordings
settings.help: With keystrokes in recordings on, also write each mouse click and where it landed.

settings.title: Watch the screen for words
settings.help: Read a text screen even when nobody is looking, and raise an alert when it says one of the phrases below. This is the case a KVM is bought for - a machine that fell over at three in the morning - so it keeps working with the console closed. Costs one pass over the frame a second, and only while the target is showing text.

settings.title: Phrases to watch for
settings.help: Comma-separated, matched without regard to case, anywhere on a line - for example: no boot device, kernel panic, press F1 to continue. An alert is raised the moment one appears and cleared when it goes, and every phrase on screen is named, not only the first; the log records both, and Home Assistant gets a sensor if MQTT is on.

settings.title: Target OS
settings.help: Which machine's conventions the console follows - the label on the Meta key, and which OS-specific key combinations it offers. "Detect" trusts the guess made from how the target enumerates USB, shown next to the USB status; set it by hand if that guess is wrong or unknown.

settings.title: Pointer mode
settings.help: Absolute puts the target's cursor exactly where you click and is the right choice almost always. Relative is for software that captures the pointer, such as games and 3D viewers, and for SteamOS in game mode, where the absolute one does not move. In relative mode the console hides your own cursor while in control, so the target's is the only one; Esc gives it back.

settings.title: Start controlling on
settings.help: "Click" waits for a click on the video before input reaches the target, and stops again on Esc or a click outside; the engaging click is still delivered. "Hover" tracks the pointer as soon as it is over the video, the way a remote desktop behaves. Keyboard input always requires a click first.

settings.title: Your cursor over the picture
settings.help: Your own cursor over the picture, while you have control in absolute mode. "arrow" is the usual one. "dot" is a small dot, so the target's own cursor is easy to see and you still know where you point. "hidden" leaves only the target's cursor, which trails yours a little.

settings.title: Whole desktop width
settings.help: For a target with more than one screen, or one that puts black borders round its picture. The absolute pointer covers the whole desktop, so with two screens the cursor runs off onto the other one, and with borders it lands short of where you click. "Find this screen" fills in these four. By hand, in the picture's pixels: for two 1920x1080 screens side by side with this one on the right, 3840, 1080, 1920, 0. For a 1440x1080 desktop in the middle of a 1920x1080 picture, 1440, 1080, -240, 0. 0 here turns it off.

settings.title: Whole desktop height
settings.help: The height of the whole desktop. 0 means the same as this screen.

settings.title: This screen's left edge
settings.help: Where this screen starts, from the left of the whole desktop. Below 0 when the desktop starts to the right of the picture's left edge (black borders).

settings.title: This screen's top edge
settings.help: Where this screen starts, from the top of the whole desktop. Below 0 when the desktop starts below the picture's top edge (black borders).

settings.title: Relative sensitivity
settings.help: Scales pointer movement in relative mode only.

settings.title: Mouse jiggler
settings.help: 0 turns it off. Otherwise the pointer is nudged one pixel and put straight back this often, so the target does not lock or fall asleep while you are watching it. It stands aside whenever you are using the mouse yourself, and does nothing when no target is attached.

settings.title: Old BIOS keyboard
settings.help: For an old BIOS that does not see the keyboard. The target then gets one plain keyboard at USB 1.1 speed, the way a real keyboard looks. The mouse, media keys and virtual media are off while this is on. Takes effect after a restart.

settings.title: Gamepad
settings.help: A game controller for the target, and a gamepad panel in the console; a controller plugged into your own computer works through it too. "Nintendo Switch": a HORI Pokken pad. "Xbox 360 (XInput)": a wired Xbox 360 pad, for Windows, a Steam Deck and Linux. "Original Xbox": the original Xbox pad, always alone; the console's controller port needs an adapter to a USB socket. The pad joins the keyboard and mouse; the "pad only" choices show the pad and nothing else, the way the real one looks - Windows needs that for the Xbox pad, and a console may ignore a pad with company. Takes effect after a restart.

settings.title: Scroll speed
settings.help: How far the target scrolls for a turn of the wheel or a swipe on a touchpad. 100 sends one wheel click per notch, 50 one per two notches.

settings.title: Target keyboard layout
settings.help: Used when pasting text, so the characters sent match what the target actually types. A KVM sends key positions, not characters.

settings.title: Paste keystroke delay
settings.help: Raise it if the target drops characters while text is being pasted.

settings.title: User key macros
settings.help: Saved macros, edited from the Input panel.

settings.title: Quick buttons
settings.help: Buttons pinned to the console's bar, edited from the Input panel.

settings.title: Runbooks
settings.help: Saved runbooks, edited from the Runbooks panel.

settings.title: Run schedules
settings.help: Let the device fire scheduled actions. It needs the clock set over the network.

settings.title: Set the clock over the network
settings.help: Recordings and screenshots are named by the clock, and schedules run by it. Without this, the console sets the clock when you sign in. Schedules set it over the network anyway.

settings.title: Time server (NTP)
settings.help: Where the clock is set from. A name on the local network works with no internet.

settings.title: Time zone
settings.help: Pick your city; the browser's own zone is at the top of the list. File names and schedules use it. Stored as a POSIX TZ string, e.g. MSK-3 or CET-1CEST,M3.5.0,M10.5.0/3.

settings.title: Clock chip
settings.help: A battery-backed clock module keeps the time through a restart with no network. Auto finds a DS3231 (or DS3231M, DS3232) and a PCF8563 or BM8563. A PCF85063 or PCF8523 shares an address with something else and must be named here. Off leaves the bus alone. Only the DS3231 has been tried on hardware.

settings.title: Clock chip wiring
settings.help: Where the module is wired. The capture board's I2C is pins 3 (SDA) and 5 (SCL) of the 40-pin header on most boards, and a DS3231 for Raspberry Pi plugs straight on there. Own pins puts it on a second I2C bus.

settings.title: Clock chip SDA
settings.help: The data line of the clock module's own bus.

settings.title: Clock chip SCL
settings.help: The clock line of the clock module's own bus.

settings.title: Schedules
settings.help: Saved schedules, edited from the Automation panel.

settings.title: Send notifications
settings.help: Push a message when a watched phrase appears or the screen goes blank.

settings.title: On a screen-watch phrase
settings.help: Notify when one of the phrases the screen is watched for appears.

settings.title: On a blank screen
settings.help: Notify when the output stays one flat colour - a stop screen, a blanked display.

settings.title: Attach a screenshot
settings.help: Send the screen with the message.

settings.title: Send dashcam clips
settings.help: When the dashcam saves a clip, send it: to Telegram as a video that plays in the chat (up to 50 MB; bigger ones are named instead), to the webhook as a message with the file's name.

settings.title: Attach recent log
settings.help: Include the tail of the device log with the message - the context around an alert.

settings.title: Telegram bot token
settings.help: From @BotFather, like 123456:AA... . Message the bot once so it may write to you.

settings.title: Telegram chat id
settings.help: The chat to message. Find chats lists the ones that wrote to the bot lately; a group or channel id typed in works too.

settings.title: Webhook URL
settings.help: A URL to POST a small JSON message to. The body is {"title":"...","message":"...","device":"<hostname>"}, with a "log" field added when the log tail is switched on above, sent as application/json; anything answering 2xx counts as delivered. Optional.

settings.title: Expose virtual media
settings.help: Present a USB drive to the target that it can boot from. Off keeps the device a plain keyboard and mouse, which also frees the USB endpoints the drive would use. Adding or removing the drive re-enumerates the device to the target, so it takes effect after a restart; swapping the image once the drive exists does not.

settings.title: Media type
settings.help: How an image is presented to the target. "Auto" serves a .iso as a CD-ROM (so it boots and mounts as an optical drive) and any other file as a removable disk - the right choice almost always. Force "CD-ROM" or "Disk" only if a file is misnamed. Handing over the whole card is picked in the Media panel, not here. Switching the type re-attaches the USB drive.

settings.title: microSD speed
settings.help: The fastest clock the card is tried at. "Auto" starts at what the board supports and steps down by itself when the card fails to mount, fails a test read, or fails a transfer later. Pick a lower one for a card that keeps stepping down. Takes effect after a restart.

settings.title: Mounted image
settings.help: File on the microSD card currently offered to the target.

settings.title: Target MAC for Wake-on-LAN
settings.help: The target's Ethernet MAC, e.g. AA:BB:CC:DD:EE:FF. The Wake button sends it a magic packet. The target must have Wake-on-LAN enabled in its BIOS and keep standby power.

settings.title: HDMI-CEC
settings.help: Talk to the target over the HDMI cable's CEC line: see what is connected, put it to sleep, wake it and send remote-control keys. Works with TV boxes, consoles, a Raspberry Pi; most PCs do not speak CEC.

settings.title: Enable ATX control
settings.help: Requires optocouplers wired to the target's front-panel header.

settings.title: Power button GPIO
settings.help: Drives the optocoupler across the target's power button. -1 to disable.

settings.title: Reset button GPIO
settings.help: Drives the optocoupler across the target's reset button. -1 to disable.

settings.title: Power LED sense GPIO
settings.help: Reads the target's power LED through an optocoupler. Wire it to the power LED, not the HDD LED, which only blinks on disk activity. -1 if you are not sensing the LED.

settings.title: HDD LED sense GPIO
settings.help: Reads the target's HDD LED the same way as the power LED, and with the same active-high setting. The power button in the console then blinks while the disk works. -1 if you are not sensing it.

settings.title: Short press
settings.help: How long a normal power or reset press is held.

settings.title: Force-off hold
settings.help: How long the power button is held for a hard power off.

settings.title: Buttons active-high
settings.help: On to press the button when the GPIO drives high (high-level-trigger optocoupler modules). Turn off if your module presses on a low.

settings.title: Power LED active-high
settings.help: On if the LED sense reads high when the target is powered. Flip it if the reported power state is inverted.

settings.title: Button GPIO
settings.help: A push button on a free pin: the M5Stack Unit Button on a Grove port (its yellow wire), or any switch to ground. -1 for none. Not tried with real hardware yet.

settings.title: A short press
settings.help: What a short press does: the target's power button, a hard power off, reset, Wake-on-LAN, a runbook (named below), saving the dashcam's last seconds as a clip, or a screenshot to the card. On a board with WiFi it can also change the connection, which restarts the device: "hotspot on/off" goes to its own hotspot and back to the mode it had, "next network mode" steps through them all, "Ethernet / WiFi" swaps the two.

settings.title: Held for 1.5 s
settings.help: What holding it does. It fires as soon as it has been held long enough, so you know it took.

settings.title: Runbook to run
settings.help: The name of the runbook, for either action set to "runbook".

settings.title: Button reads high when pressed
settings.help: Off for a button that connects the pin to ground, which is the usual kind and the M5Stack Unit Button. On for one that connects it to 3V3.

settings.title: Serial console
settings.help: The target's serial port, for a machine with no screen at all - a NAS, a router, a server - or one that shows its BIOS over serial. Wire the target's TX to the RX pin below and its RX to the TX pin, plus ground. 3.3 V logic (a Raspberry Pi, a router's header) goes straight in; a real RS-232 port (9-pin, +-12 V) needs a MAX3232 module in between, or it damages the pin.

settings.title: Serial port over USB
settings.help: A serial port on the USB cable the target already has, so no wires. Linux sees it as /dev/ttyACM0, Windows as a COM port, macOS as /dev/cu.usbmodem*. "Serial console": the serial console uses it instead of the pins below; on Linux run a login on it with "systemctl enable --now serial-getty@ttyACM0". "Agent": it is for espkvm-agent, a small program on the target that shows what the machine is and shares its clipboard. Not together with a gamepad. Takes effect after a restart.

settings.title: TX pin (to the target's RX)
settings.help: The GPIO this device sends on. -1 until you pick one.

settings.title: RX pin (from the target's TX)
settings.help: The GPIO this device listens on. -1 until you pick one.

settings.title: Speed (baud)
settings.help: What the target's console runs at; 115200 for Linux and most boards, 9600 or 115200 for a PC BIOS. Always 8 data bits, no parity, one stop bit.

settings.title: HDMI audio
settings.help: The capture board sends the HDMI sound as I2S on three wires: bit clock (BCLK or SCK), word clock (WS, LRCK or WFS) and data (SD or DATA). Wire them to three free pins, plus ground, and pick those pins below. On the Geekworm C790 they are on the J4 header.

settings.title: BCLK pin (bit clock)
settings.help: -1 until you pick one.

settings.title: WS pin (word clock)
settings.help: -1 until you pick one.

settings.title: DATA pin
settings.help: -1 until you pick one.

settings.title: Hostname
settings.help: Also the mDNS name: <hostname>.local

settings.title: Say on the network that this is an ESP-KVM
settings.help: Adds the product and the board to the mDNS announcement, and an _espkvm._tcp service, so a discovery tool or a script can find every ESP-KVM on the network. Off, only the hostname is announced. The firmware version is never announced.

settings.title: IPv6
settings.help: Also answer on an IPv6 address, alongside IPv4. There is nothing to configure: the address comes from the router's advertisements. Turn it off to keep the device off IPv6 entirely.

settings.title: Connection
settings.help: "Ethernet": the wired port. "WiFi": join the network below (Ethernet is left down). "Own hotspot": the device makes its own WiFi hotspot for setup where there is no network to join. "Ethernet, WiFi as backup": the wired port, with the WiFi network below joined and waiting - when the cable is pulled the device moves to WiFi, and back when the cable returns. It answers on both addresses. If WiFi is unreachable: reset the board, then hold the button for two seconds - that returns it to Ethernet, and clears the password too. Hold it AFTER the reset, not through it.

settings.title: WiFi network (SSID)
settings.help: The name of the network to join in WiFi mode.

settings.title: WiFi password
settings.help: Left blank for an open network. Stored write-only.

settings.title: Open hotspot (no password)
settings.help: Run the device's hotspot with no password at all. Off, and with no password set, the device makes one up on first use and prints it in the log and on the display - an open network anybody in the building can join is a poor way to reach a server. Turn this on only where that is what you want.

settings.title: Hotspot password
settings.help: Password for the device's own hotspot ("Own hotspot" mode, or the rescue hotspot below). At least 8 characters. Left blank, the device makes one up the first time the hotspot comes up and prints it in the log and on the display; for a hotspot with no password at all, use the setting above. The network name is ESP-KVM-xxxx (the device's MAC). Stored write-only.

settings.title: If WiFi can't connect
settings.help: "Keep trying": keep retrying the network - it reconnects on its own when the network comes back (best for a device you cannot reach physically). "Also start a hotspot": ALSO run a rescue hotspot (ESP-KVM-xxxx) the whole time WiFi is trying, so you can always reach the device on-site to fix its settings - set a Hotspot password first. Only applies in WiFi (station) mode.

settings.title: Setup hotspot on an unclaimed device
settings.help: While no password has been set and no network cable is plugged in, put out an open hotspot (ESP-KVM-xxxx) so the device can be reached and given one. It stops happening the moment a password exists. Until then a visitor can only set that password - video, keyboard and every other endpoint stay shut.

settings.title: Receive the target's log
settings.help: Listen for the target's kernel messages over the network: Linux netconsole, or anything that sends plain syslog over UDP. It keeps working when the target's disk is gone, which is when you want it. On the target, for example: modprobe netconsole netconsole=@/,6666@<this device's IP>/. What arrives is unauthenticated UDP - anyone on the network can read it or send lines - so it is kept as text and can only raise a notification, never run anything.

settings.title: UDP port
settings.help: 6666 is netconsole's usual port; 514 is syslog's.

settings.title: Accept from
settings.help: The target's IP address; several separated by commas. Empty accepts lines from anyone on the network.

settings.title: Alert on
settings.help: Comma-separated phrases, matched without regard to case. A line holding one sends a notification, at most one every 30 seconds. Empty for none.

settings.title: Enable WireGuard
settings.help: Bring up a classic WireGuard tunnel to a hub so the device is reachable over the VPN. Off by default. Split-tunnel: only the tunnel subnet goes through WireGuard, so the console stays reachable on the LAN too. An alternative to Tailscale below, not a companion - enable one.

settings.title: Tunnel address
settings.help: The device's own IP on the WireGuard network, e.g. 10.9.0.2.

settings.title: Private key
settings.help: Base64 WireGuard private key. Leave empty and the device generates one on first connect; its public key is shown below.

settings.title: Peer public key
settings.help: Base64 public key of the WireGuard peer (the hub/server).

settings.title: Peer endpoint
settings.help: host:port of the peer, e.g. vpn.example.com:51820.

settings.title: Persistent keepalive
settings.help: Keeps a NAT/firewall mapping open. 25 is typical; 0 disables it.

settings.title: Sync time over SNTP
settings.help: WireGuard handshakes carry a timestamp; without a real clock a reboot can make the peer reject them. Turn this on if the device can reach an NTP server. Off by default (isolated networks).

settings.title: NTP server
settings.help: Used only when SNTP is on.

settings.title: Enable Tailscale
settings.help: Join a Tailscale network natively - the device gets a 100.x address reachable from anywhere on your tailnet, with NAT traversal handled for you and no separate gateway. Off by default. An alternative to WireGuard above, not a companion; enabling both is unusual.

settings.title: Auth key
settings.help: Optional. A Tailscale auth key (tskey-auth-...) that authorises this device to join. Empty, the device shows a link to sign in with your Tailscale account instead. Generate a key in the Tailscale admin console; a reusable key survives re-registration across reboots.

settings.title: Tailnet hostname
settings.help: The name this device takes on the tailnet. Empty uses the mDNS hostname from the Network section.

settings.title: Console only over Tailscale
settings.help: While the device is on the tailnet, the console answers only to tailnet addresses (100.64.0.0/10). The setup hotspot still works, and while Tailscale is down the console answers everywhere again, so a broken tailnet cannot lock you out.

settings.title: Sign in these tailnet users
settings.help: Tailscale logins, separated by commas (alice@example.com). A browser on a device of one of these users is signed in as the owner without a password or a code. Works once a password of your own is set. Signing out there signs straight back in.

settings.title: Let these tailnet users watch
settings.help: Tailscale logins, separated by commas. These are signed in as the viewer: they see the screen and cannot type, click or change anything.

settings.title: Control server
settings.help: Coordination server for a self-hosted control plane (Headscale, Ionscale). Empty uses Tailscale's own (controlplane.tailscale.com). A host (headscale.example.com) or a URL (https://headscale.example.com:8443), which then sets TLS and the port too.

settings.title: Control server port
settings.help: Port for the control server. 0 = default (443 with TLS, else 80). Set only if your Headscale listens on a non-standard port.

settings.title: Control plane over TLS
settings.help: Reach the coordination server over HTTPS. Required for the hosted Tailscale service (the default). Turn off only for a self-hosted Headscale served over plain HTTP.

settings.title: Warn before the key runs out
settings.help: Send a notification this many days before the tailnet key expires. Tailscale gives a node six months at most, and when that runs out the device drops off the tailnet until someone authorises it again. 0 turns the warning off. Needs notifications set up and the clock in sync.

settings.title: Trusted certificate (Let's Encrypt)
settings.help: Get a Let's Encrypt certificate for the device's tailnet name (host.tailnet.ts.net) and renew it on its own, so a browser trusts the console with nothing imported. Needs MagicDNS and HTTPS certificates turned on in the Tailscale admin console (DNS page). The name is published in Certificate Transparency logs. The local name and the IP addresses keep the device's own certificate.

settings.title: Publish to MQTT
settings.help: Report status to an MQTT broker and appear in Home Assistant (auto-discovered). Off by default; costs nothing when off.

settings.title: Broker host
settings.help: Hostname or IP of the MQTT broker, e.g. the Home Assistant host.

settings.title: Broker port
settings.help: 1883 for plain MQTT, 8883 for MQTT over TLS.

settings.title: Use TLS
settings.help: Connect with mqtts. Set the port to 8883 as well.

settings.title: Verify broker certificate
settings.help: With TLS on, check the broker's certificate against the built-in CA bundle (public CAs, e.g. Let's Encrypt). Turn off for a broker with a self-signed certificate.

settings.title: Username
settings.help: Leave empty for an anonymous broker.

settings.title: Password
settings.help: Stored on the device; never sent back to the console.

settings.title: Base topic
settings.help: Topic prefix; the device id is appended, e.g. espkvm/a1b2c3.

settings.title: Discovery prefix
settings.help: Home Assistant MQTT discovery prefix. Default suits a stock HA.

settings.title: Publish interval
settings.help: How often telemetry is published.

settings.title: Send a picture with a screen alert
settings.help: When the screen watch fires, publish a still of the screen as a camera in Home Assistant, so the notification carries what the machine actually shows. The button is always there; this only decides whether an alert takes a picture by itself. Needs the MJPEG codec - there is no still to take while H.264 runs - and a 1080p frame is a few hundred kilobytes over the broker.

settings.title: Serve over HTTPS
settings.help: Uses a self-signed certificate generated on first boot. Disable only on a trusted network or behind a VPN.

settings.title: Agent REST API
settings.help: Enables the plain-REST snapshot and keyboard/mouse endpoints (/api/v1/video/frame.jpg, /api/v1/hid/*) used to drive the target from an AI agent or a script. Off by default: it grants the same control the console already has, over a simpler interface, so turn it on only when you mean to hand that control to a program.

settings.title: Offer firmware updates
settings.help: The browser asks the address below whether a newer build exists and offers to install it. With the project's own address it also tells check.espkvm.io, at most once a day, this device's random id, its board, its version and the chip revision, so the author can count the devices in use. The id is not taken from the hardware; a settings reset makes a new one. The device never reaches out on its own - a KVM that phones home is not what belongs in an isolated network.

settings.title: Update manifest
settings.help: URL of a manifest.json describing the newest build. The project's own builds are published at the default address; point it at your fork, or at a file server inside your network, and it will use that instead. Whatever it points at is what gets written to the device, so point it somewhere you trust.

settings.title: Let the device fetch releases itself
settings.help: Off by default, and deliberately so: a KVM often sits where nothing is supposed to reach the internet, and it does not talk to GitHub unless it is told to. Turn it on and the console can offer any published release - which is how you go back to an earlier one, since the browser is not allowed to download the image itself. Ordinary updates do not need this; the browser fetches those and hands them over.

settings.title: Thermal protection
settings.help: Cap the frame rate when the chip gets warm and stop encoding if it gets hot. Keyboard, mouse and the web interface keep running either way - a KVM that stops accepting keystrokes because it is warm has failed at its job.

settings.title: Warm threshold
settings.help: Above this the frame rate is halved. Measured on this board: 1080p MJPEG at full rate settles around 46 C in open air, so the default leaves plenty of room before anything is given up.

settings.title: Hot threshold
settings.help: Above this encoding stops until the chip cools. The ESP32 family is rated to 85 C ambient and the die runs hotter than the air around it.

settings.title: Panel side
settings.help: Which side of the screen the button rail and its panels sit on.

settings.title: Show the keys sent
settings.help: The last few keys and key combinations that went to the target, in the bottom bar. Handy when the target seems to ignore a key, or to show someone what you press.

settings.title: Hide the bars in full screen
settings.help: In full screen the status strip, the rail and the bottom bar slide away and the picture takes the whole screen. They come back over it with the mouse at an edge (after a moment while you have control), the small tab at the top, or a tap of the right Ctrl key on its own, and go again a few seconds after you leave them.

settings.title: Keyboard button
settings.help: What the keyboard button under the picture opens in touch mode. "Console" is the console's own keyboard, with Ctrl, Alt, the F keys and the arrows a phone's keyboard does not have. "Phone" is the phone's own keyboard, for typing text with its layouts and suggestions.

settings.title: Shown in the console
settings.help: Untick a control to take its button out of the console, for everyone who signs in. It only hides the button: the feature itself stays as its own settings have it. Stored as the ids of the hidden controls; the console keeps the list of what can be hidden.

settings.title: On key presses
settings.help: A short tick under the finger on each press of the on-screen keyboard, the arrow keys and the gamepad buttons, like a phone's own keyboard. Android only: Safari on an iPhone cannot vibrate.

settings.title: On the touchpad
settings.help: In touch mode, a faint tick every few millimetres the finger travels, the way the touchpads of the Steam Controller feel. Half the strength of a key press.

settings.title: Strength
settings.help: A browser cannot set how strong a vibration is, only how long, so stronger means a longer tick: about 12, 25 or 45 ms.

settings.title: Status display
settings.help: Drive a small display that shows the IP, link, capture status and health. An I2C OLED (SSD1306/SH1106) shares the capture chip's I2C and is auto-detected with no extra pins; a round SPI LCD (GC9A01) uses the GPIOs set below, after you pick it as the display type. Off by default; does nothing when no panel is connected.

settings.title: Panel
settings.help: Which panel is wired, controller and size together. SSD1306 and SH1106 are I2C OLEDs - pick SH1106 if the image is shifted by two pixels or wraps. GC9A01 is a round colour SPI LCD, e.g. the Waveshare 1.28" module. None of this can be detected: one chip drives every size and reports none of it. A wrong size shows the picture squeezed into part of the glass, or every other row missing. Shorter panels show fewer status lines.

settings.title: Upside down
settings.help: Turn the picture on the status display through 180 degrees, for a panel mounted the other way up because of where its connector or its enclosure put it. Takes effect at once: the panel is re-initialised where it stands, with no restart.

settings.title: LCD SCLK / CLK
settings.help: SPI clock GPIO for the GC9A01. Ignored by the I2C OLEDs.

settings.title: LCD MOSI / DIN
settings.help: SPI data GPIO for the GC9A01.

settings.title: LCD CS
settings.help: Chip-select GPIO for the GC9A01.

settings.title: LCD DC
settings.help: Data/command GPIO for the GC9A01.

settings.title: LCD RST
settings.help: Reset GPIO for the GC9A01. -1 (None) if RST is tied to 3V3.

settings.title: OLED SDA
settings.help: I2C data GPIO for an OLED on a bus of its own, such as the Grove port of the M5Stack Unit PoE-P4. -1 (None) puts the OLED on the capture chip's bus, where most boards have it. Set both SDA and SCL, or neither.

settings.title: OLED SCL
settings.help: I2C clock GPIO for an OLED on a bus of its own. -1 (None) puts it on the capture chip's bus.

settings.title: LCD backlight
settings.help: Backlight GPIO for the GC9A01. -1 (None) if BL is tied to 3V3 (always on).
